name: Trae

surfaces.label: TRAE SOLO CN standalone app (SOLO mode split out of the IDE). Bundle id NOT known; path inferred from the app data folder name 'TRAE SOLO CN' (agentsview) and an optional CLI path in openai/codex#22629. The folder name has spaces, so the probe sees argv[0]='/Applications/TRAE' then 'SOLO' then 'CN.app/Contents/MacOS/...'. Listed before the IDE surfaces because the probe keeps the first surface that matches. Inferred, never seen. TraeWork Desktop (the newer standalone client) has no known bundle id or path and has no rule.

TRAE IDE, international edition (TraeCode, VS Code fork, Electron). /Applications/Trae.app, bundle id com.trae.app (Homebrew cask trae). Helper processes have spaces in their path ('Trae Helper (Plugin)'), so their argv[0] splits to '.../Frameworks/Trae' and does not match; only the main process does. One process hosts every chat and agent, so this is a host: report the app, never map it to one transcript.

TRAE CN IDE (China edition). /Applications/Trae CN.app, bundle id cn.trae.app (Homebrew cask trae-cn), main binary reported as Electron. Space in the folder name: argv[0] splits to '/Applications/Trae' and the next argument is 'CN.app/Contents/MacOS/Electron'. Same host caveat as the international edition.

traecli acp: the CLI run as an Agent Client Protocol server for an editor or client (TraeCode CLI 2.0 docs: `acp` subcommand; TRAE CLI 1.0 uses `traecli acp serve`). Listed before the tui surface, which vetoes the same argument.
traecli app-server: TraeCode CLI 2.0 app server for remote TUI connections (`--remote ws://host:port`). Codex-fork shape, so it likely hosts many threads in one process. Never seen.

TRAE CLI in a terminal: TraeCode CLI 2.0 (a closed-source codex-rs fork, also called TraeX) or TRAE CLI 1.0 (older, yaml config). Native binary; argv[0] basename is traecli, traex or trae-cli (the 1.0 installer puts traecli in ~/.local/bin). Vetoed on subcommands that are not sessions. `exec` and `review` are one-shot runs: alive means working. The old internal name coco is not matched (only third-party evidence).

trae-agent, the open-source Python CLI (github.com/bytedance/trae-agent): `trae-cli run "task"` or `trae-cli interactive`. It is a Python console script, so ps shows the interpreter with the script path as argument (observed locally with a shebang script: argv[0] is the interpreter, then <prefix>/bin/trae-cli); argv[0] is never 'trae-cli'. The rule matches the '/bin/trae-cli' script path, not the bare word, so `python serve.py` inside a folder called trae-cli-notes and `pip install trae-cli` do not match. Interpreter names cover venv, uv and macOS framework Python ('Python'). `run` is one-shot: alive means working. `interactive` idles at a prompt. The name trae-cli is also the TraeX alias above; the split is argv[0] (native binary) versus interpreter plus script argument (Python).
trae-agent started as a module: `python -m trae_agent.cli run ...` (cli.py has a __main__ guard). Same one-shot and interactive behaviour as the console-script surface.

working_signals.meaning: trae-agent only: its bash tool starts a persistent /bin/bash child (create_subprocess_shell('/bin/bash'); on macOS the wrapping sh execs bash, so ps shows a direct child named bash, observed locally) on the first bash tool call and closes it when the task ends (_close_tools), so a shell child that is a DIRECT child of the python process means a task is running. Absent before the first bash call and while the model is thinking. TraeX and the IDE: no such rule. Not present when trae-agent runs its tools inside Docker (--docker-image and friends): then no local shell child exists.

TraeX rollout JSONL (Codex-compatible, inferred; only when the process carries --resume <id>, since a fresh session has no id in argv). Raises working, absence proves nothing: the Codex row measured in-turn gaps up to 528 s. trae-agent rewrites its whole trajectory JSON at start, after every LLM reply and every step, but the file is under the LAUNCH cwd (or -t path), not under the process cwd, and has no session id, so the probe cannot reach it.
fallback, an unmeasured guess. A turn waiting on the model burns no CPU. For the IDE (Electron plus editor and language servers) never use CPU as the only reason.

waiting_signals.meaning: official docs: the agent is waiting for the user. notification_type idle_prompt means the agent finished the task, not that it is blocked. Hooks need ~/.trae/hooks.json (or a Claude Code settings.json import) and, per a third-party changelog (CodeIsland, not the official page), global hooks turned on in the TRAE settings.

Codex-compatible hook events (third-party: tmux-scout registers PermissionRequest and Notification for traex). Hooks are inert until trusted in the startup prompt or /hooks. Not in the official 2.0 docs.
snake_case events in the yaml hooks: section (third-party: tmux-scout coco.js). Also notification and stop. Not in the official 1.0 docs.
trae-agent has no approval prompt at all. The only human wait is the `interactive` input prompt between tasks, which is idle, not blocked.

hooks.config: IDE: ~/.trae/hooks.json (global) or <project>/.trae/hooks.json, format {version:1, hooks:{Event:[{matcher, hooks:[{type:command, command, timeout}]}]}}; also reads Claude Code hooks from ~/.claude/settings.json. TraeCode CLI 2.0: Codex-compatible hooks and plugins, trusted through a startup prompt or /hooks; config location not in the official docs (third-party says ~/.trae/traecli.toml with [features].hooks=true, another says ~/.trae/cli/hooks.json). TRAE CLI 1.0: hooks: section in the yaml config (third-party). trae-agent: none.

telemetry.how: Unknown for every surface except trae-agent, which has none (source grep). Not documented for the IDE or either CLI generation. trae-agent source has no OpenTelemetry (grep for otel, opentelemetry, telemetry finds nothing). The TraeCode CLI 2.0 config reference lists only model, approval_policy, default_permissions, trae_login_base_url, projects and mcp_servers. TraeX is a codex-rs fork and upstream Codex has an [otel] table, but nothing confirms Trae kept it. Not determined for the IDE.

sources.claim: the process rules were run through the probe's matches() on 27 synthetic argv lines; the python console-script shape was checked against a real shebang script
sources.evidence: tools/agents_probe.py matches() on lines for Trae.app, Trae CN.app, TRAE SOLO CN.app main and helper processes, traecli/traex with and without subcommands, python scripts. `ps -axo pid=,args=` for a script `#!<python> ` named bin/trae-cli printed '<Python> <dir>/bin/trae-cli run fix it' (argv[0] is the interpreter). asyncio.create_subprocess_shell('/bin/bash') printed a direct child '/bin/bash' (no sh).

notes: Trae is not one program. (1) trae-agent: the open-source Python research CLI at the URL given as a hint; it is a script run by an interpreter. (2) TRAE IDE, and TRAE CN: Electron VS Code forks, one process hosting every agent. (3) TraeCode CLI, command traecli (1.0 yaml, 2.0 a closed codex-rs fork also called TraeX), the terminal agent people usually mean. (4) Standalone SOLO and TraeWork apps. The most precise turn signal differs per surface: trae-agent, a shell child that lives for the task (or process alive for `run`); IDE, the UserPromptSubmit to Stop hook pair; TraeX, a rollout with no task_complete (inferred); CLI 1.0, nothing outside hooks. Nothing was seen live, so every floor and window is a guess. The probe splits ps on spaces, so 'Trae CN.app' and 'TRAE SOLO CN.app' match on split fragments. Verified 2026-09-29 by an adversarial pass: known false positives that the schema cannot remove are the IDE launchers (`trae`/`trae-cn --goto`, which VS Code forks implement by running the app's Electron binary in node mode, so a brief process matches the IDE surface; inferred), and prompt words that equal a deny-listed subcommand (ps splits on spaces, so `traecli exec update the docs` is vetoed). `traecli --cd <dir with acp in its name>` is filed under the daemon surface. Inferred parts: the SOLO CN app path, the TraeX session store layout, the process name of the 2.0 binary, every CPU floor and window.
